open-question.question: The side-bar view is a native VS Code tree listing every live mission, and each mission must show its title, the workflow step to run next, its count of open questions, its count of remaining tasks, and a marker while a run is going. A tree item offers a label, a description, a tooltip, an icon, and child rows. Which of these carries each of the five facts, and is a mission's row a leaf or does it expand into child rows?
open-question.alternative: A mission's row is a leaf with no child rows. The label carries the mission's title. The description carries the next workflow step's name followed by both counts in a compact form, for example "Derive tasks · 3 questions · 2 tasks". The icon carries the running marker: a spinning ThemeIcon while the mission's run is going and a steady mission icon otherwise. The tooltip repeats all five facts spelled out in full, beside the mission's path. Every fact the goal names is visible at a glance on one line per mission, using each TreeItem field for what VS Code draws it for. The list stays as long as the number of live missions, and the spinner is the editor's own idiom for work in progress. The description is the first text the editor truncates in a narrow side bar, so the counts, which come last, are the first to be cut off. The step name and two counts have to share one short dimmed string, which pushes toward abbreviations a person must learn.

A mission's row is a leaf with no child rows. The label carries the title. The icon carries the next workflow step as one ThemeIcon chosen per step (first review round, additional review round, derive tasks, execute tasks, finish), and while a run is going it is replaced by a spinning icon, which is how the running marker shows. The description carries only the two counts, for example "3 questions · 2 tasks". The tooltip names the step in words, the two counts, whether a run is going, and the path. The description stays short enough to survive a narrow side bar, and the step reads at a glance once its icons are known, which leaves the row's text for the counts. A person has to learn what each step's icon means, and until then needs the tooltip. While a run is going the spinner hides which step the mission is on. Choosing five or more codicons that read clearly as workflow steps is a design task of its own, and an icon on its own is not announced as a step name by a screen reader unless accessibility information is set.

A mission's row is a leaf with no child rows and no icon. The label carries the title. The description carries every other fact as text: a "running" word in front while a run is going, then the next step's name, then the two counts. The tooltip repeats the facts in full beside the path. Every fact is a word a person or a screen reader can read, with no icon meaning to learn, and the row needs no choice of codicons. The description is now holding four facts, so it truncates soonest of all the leaf layouts, and the running marker, which comes first, pushes the counts further toward the cut. A word is also much less noticeable than a spinner when scanning which missions are busy.

A mission's row is a leaf with no child rows. The label carries the title, the description carries only the next step's name, and the icon carries the running marker as a spinning icon while a run is going. The two counts appear only in the tooltip, beside the step, the running state, and the path. The row is the cleanest and least likely to truncate, showing what most decides the next action, which mission and which step, and whether it is busy. The counts are seen only on hover, which arguably falls short of the goal's statement that the tree lists each mission with its counts of open questions and remaining tasks, and a person cannot compare missions' counts by scanning the list.

A mission's row expands into child rows. The collapsed row carries the title in its label, the next step in its description, and the running marker as a spinning icon. Its children are one row per count, "Open questions" and "Remaining tasks", each with its number in the description, and these children are plain rows with no further children. The tooltip of the mission row repeats all the facts with the path. The counts are shown in full words on rows of their own, never abbreviated or truncated, while the collapsed row still shows the step and whether a run is going. With missions expanded the list is three times as long, and with them collapsed the counts are hidden, so the counts are either costly in space or not visible at a glance. The extension also has to choose and keep a collapsed or expanded default per mission, and the child rows carry information a click on them does nothing with.

A mission's row expands into two child group rows, "Open questions" and "Remaining tasks", each showing its count in its description and expanding in turn into one row per open question title or per remaining task heading, read from the documents the extension already reads. The collapsed mission row carries the title in its label, the next step and both counts in its description, and the running marker as a spinning icon; the tooltip repeats all the facts with the path. The counts are visible both on the collapsed row and on the group rows, and expanding a mission lets a person browse what is open and left without opening its window, which uses the question and task lists the extension already holds. It adds a second view of the questions and tasks beside the mission window's own two panes, beyond what the goal asks the side bar to show, with deeper rows whose clicks need a meaning and whose contents must be kept fresh on every file event. The collapsed row still carries the step and both counts in one description, so it truncates like the one-line leaf.

open-question.question: The side-bar view is a native VS Code tree and must carry the four controls that belong to no mission: New mission, Define mission, Refresh, and Settings. On today's page New mission and Define mission are buttons whose label shows the harness, model, and effort of the variant they run, each with a dropdown beside it that selects among its recipe's variants, and a native tree view holds neither a labelled button nor a dropdown. Where in the side-bar view does each of the four controls sit, and how do New mission and Define mission there show the variant they will run and let a person select another?
open-question.alternative: All four controls are icon actions in the side-bar view's title bar (`menus` `view/title`, `navigation` group), so none of them is a tree row. Refresh and Settings run at once. New mission and Define mission each open a VS Code QuickPick of their recipe's variants, every entry labelled with its harness, model, and effort, the variant remembered in `gurita.projectVariantSelections` listed first and marked; accepting an entry remembers it and then asks for the goal (and scope) as today. Nothing shows the variant before the click. It uses the editor's own place for view-wide actions and adds no row to the tree, so the controls stand unchanged whether the view lists missions, lists none, or shows its failure state, and every variant stays one pick away. The variant a click will run is visible only after clicking, since a title-bar action's tooltip is its static command title, and every start costs an extra confirming step even when the remembered variant is wanted.

All four controls are icon actions in the side-bar view's title bar. New mission and Define mission run the remembered variant directly, showing it nowhere in the side-bar; the two dropdowns that select it move into the Settings window, which already lists the variants. Starting a mission is one click on a conventional title-bar icon, and the selection lives beside the variants and harness settings it draws from, so the side-bar needs no variant mechanism at all. A person cannot see from the side-bar which harness, model, and effort a click will run, and changing it means opening another window, which undoes the at-a-glance label the fixed-name buttons carry today.

Refresh and Settings are icon actions in the view's title bar. New mission and Define mission are two tree rows standing above the mission rows, each labelled with its control's name, its `description` showing the remembered variant's harness, model, and effort. Clicking the row runs that variant; an inline icon action on the row, also offered in its context menu, opens a QuickPick of the recipe's variants that changes the remembered selection without starting a run. It keeps today's two properties together: the variant a click will run is visible before clicking, and starting with it is one click, while selecting another stays on the row itself. Two non-mission rows share the tree with the missions and must also be drawn when no mission is live or the read fails, which bears on how the sibling empty and failure states are drawn, and the hover-only inline action is less discoverable than today's visible dropdown.

Refresh and Settings are icon actions in the view's title bar. New mission and Define mission are two tree rows above the mission rows, each `description` showing the remembered variant's harness, model, and effort. Clicking a row always opens the QuickPick of its recipe's variants with the remembered one preselected; accepting runs it and remembers it. The variant is visible before the click and a different one is chosen in the same gesture that starts the run, with no separate action to find. Every start takes a second confirming step even when the shown variant is wanted, and the rows still have to stand in the tree beside the missions in every state of the view.

Refresh and Settings are icon actions in the view's title bar. New mission and Define mission are two collapsible tree rows above the mission rows, each `description` showing the remembered variant. Clicking the row runs the remembered variant; expanding it shows one child row per variant of its recipe, labelled with harness, model, and effort, the remembered one marked by its icon, and clicking a child runs that variant and makes it the remembered one. Every variant is visible and runnable with one click inside the tree's own structure, the closest a native tree comes to today's dropdown without a QuickPick. An expanded control row can push the missions far down the list when a recipe carries many variants, and conflating expansion with selection makes the tree's twisty behave unlike every mission row's, which also depends on how the sibling row-layout question uses child rows.

Refresh and Settings are icon actions in the view's title bar. New mission and Define mission are two tree rows above the mission rows, each `description` showing the remembered variant's harness, model, and effort, and clicking a row runs it. The side-bar offers no way to select another variant: the two dropdowns move into the Settings window. The variant is visible and runs in one click, and the side-bar carries no selection mechanism of its own, keeping the tree's rows simple. Changing the variant requires opening the Settings window, a detour today's dropdown beside the button does not need, and the rows still stand among the missions in every state of the view.

All four controls are tree rows grouped above the mission rows: Refresh and Settings as labelled rows that act on click, New mission and Define mission as rows whose `description` shows the remembered variant, run on click, and offer an inline action and context-menu entry opening the variant QuickPick that changes the selection. The view's title bar carries no action. Every control is labelled and visible in the same list, so nothing depends on recognising a title-bar icon or hovering for an inline action. Four rows that belong to no mission crowd the list and scroll away with it, Refresh and Settings sit outside the place VS Code users look for view-wide actions, and all four must be drawn in the empty and failure states as well.

The side-bar container holds a second view, a `WebviewViewProvider` webview above the mission tree, drawing New mission and Define mission as today's labelled buttons with a variant dropdown beside each, reused from the page script; Refresh and Settings are icon actions in the tree view's title bar. The mission tree carries no control rows. It keeps today's labelled buttons and dropdowns exactly, both visible and one click, and leaves the tree for missions alone. It departs from the goal's one native tree carrying the four controls and would need the goal revised first, and it adds a second webview with its own content security policy, script, and message protocol to build and test.

All four controls are icon actions in the view's title bar, and for now the side-bar offers no variant display or selection: New mission and Define mission run the variant remembered in `gurita.projectVariantSelections`, or the recipe's first variant when none is remembered, and a selection mechanism is added in a later mission. It is the least to build now, keeping this mission on the side-bar, the windows, and the icon rather than on a replacement for the dropdown. It drops the variant label and dropdown that the started recipe-variants mission has just landed on the fixed-name buttons, so a person cannot see or change which harness a new mission starts under until the later work lands.

open-question.question: Today's mission pane shows the line `No mission is live.` when no mission is live, and one failure state naming the cause when the read of the live missions fails. Once the missions are listed in a native side-bar tree, how does that view show each of those two states, in which it has no mission row to draw?
open-question.alternative: Both states are drawn through the tree view's own `message` property (`TreeView.message`), with the tree returning no rows. With no mission live the message is today's line `No mission is live.`. When the live read fails it is today's failure line `The live missions could not be read.` followed by the cause as the read gave it. A successful read with missions clears the message. Nothing is added to the manifest, and the view's other contents (its title-bar controls included) stay as they are in every state. One dynamic surface serves both states. It sits in the view itself, carries the cause verbatim exactly as the pane's failure state does today, is set and cleared from the same code path that answers each live read, and needs no manifest entry, context key, or extra command, so a stub of the `vscode` module can cover it by recording one property. The message is one plain-text string rendered above the tree, with no Markdown, link, or button. A long or multi-line cause (a Python traceback or git's message) is shown cramped or cut short in a narrow side bar. Neither state offers an action in the body of the view, so with no mission live a person finds New mission and Define mission only where the sibling question on the side-bar controls places them.

Both states are drawn as tree rows that are not missions, returned by the tree data provider in place of mission rows. With no mission live the provider returns one row labelled `No mission is live.`, with no command. When the live read fails it returns one row labelled with the failure line and an error `ThemeIcon`, the cause carried in the row's tooltip and also as non-clickable child rows, one per line of the cause, so expanding the row shows it whole. Each placeholder row carries its own `contextValue`, so no mission menu or click handler applies to it. Everything stays inside the one tree data provider and the one tree. The cause can be shown in full, line by line, however long it is, and can be inspected or copied from the tooltip. No manifest welcome entry, context key, or second rendering mechanism is needed. A placeholder row looks like any other row, so it reads as something to click or expand. Every piece of code that handles rows (the click that opens a mission's window, row menus, the running marker, and the counts) has to tell placeholder rows from mission rows. Any row layout the sibling question on mission rows settles (for example, whether rows expand) has to be kept from leaking into the placeholders. The view also loses VS Code's own empty-view look.

Both states are drawn as `viewsWelcome` content contributed in the manifest for the view. It shows only while the tree has no rows, and the extension picks which entry shows by setting a context key with `setContext` (for example, none live versus read failed). The no-mission entry reads `No mission is live.`. The failure entry reads `The live missions could not be read.`, but its text is static manifest text and cannot hold the cause. So the cause is written to an output channel the extension contributes, and the failure entry carries a command link or button that reveals that channel. Either entry may also carry command links in Markdown, such as Refresh. This is VS Code's native idiom for an empty view. Its Markdown, links, and buttons can put the next action (refreshing, or starting a mission) right in the body of the view, and the extension keeps no extra rows or message text. The cause is no longer in the view itself: a person has to follow a link to an output channel, unlike today's failure state, which names the cause on the page. The approach adds a manifest entry per state, a context key that must be kept true to every read (so the wrong entry never shows, including before the first read lands), an output channel, and a command, and the editor-stub tests cover none of that content. Any button for New mission or Define mission placed in the welcome entries overlaps the axis the sibling question on the side-bar controls owns.

Each open mission window keeps the page it last drew, diagram, recipes, preview, and both panes as they stood, with a notice above it naming the cause and saying the page is as of the last successful read; every action button on the page is drawn disabled, as it is today while a run is going, until a live read succeeds and the page is drawn afresh. The person keeps reading the mission's questions and tasks through the fault, while no run can start from a page whose step, state, or very liveness the failed read could not confirm, and the disabled-button drawing already exists for running missions. Each open mission window keeps the page it last drew with a notice above it naming the cause, and its actions stay enabled, so a click runs its recipe against the mission's path as the last successful read gave it. Every click is today checked against what the latest answer posted, and here the latest answer is a failure, so the extension must accept clicks against a stale page; a run can start for a mission that has since been finished or whose next step has moved, the person warned only by the notice.

The mission windows change nothing when the live read fails: each keeps the page it last drew, with no notice and its actions as they were, and the failure is shown only where the side-bar view shows it, the windows being redrawn on the next read that succeeds. It needs no failure drawing, per-window state, or message in the mission windows at all, and a short-lived fault never disturbs the page a person is working in. Nothing in the window says its page may be stale or that the extension cannot currently read the missions, so a person working in a window with the side-bar hidden acts on a page the extension no longer vouches for; it rests on the side-bar view showing the failure, which the sibling question on the side-bar view without missions settles.

Each open mission window stops relying on the failed live read for its content: it re-reads its own mission's `open_questions.xml` and `TASKS_TODO.md` in process, as `src/documents.ts` already does apart from `missions.py live`, and draws the panes from that fresh read, each with its own notice where its file is missing or does not parse, while the workflow diagram shows no step to run next, since `nextStep` needs the started or defined state only the live read gives; a notice names the cause, and every action button is drawn disabled until a live read succeeds. The panes stay current through the fault, a question answered or a task completed still showing, because the documents do not depend on the read that failed, while no run starts without the state the step choice needs. A window reads its mission's files apart from any confirmation that the mission is still live, so a directory removed by finishing reads as missing files rather than an ended mission, and the window must draw a partial page (panes without a step) that no state of today's page has; its reads depend on the watching that the read and watch lifetime question settles.

Each open mission window re-reads its own mission's `open_questions.xml` and `TASKS_TODO.md` in process and draws the panes from that fresh read, the diagram showing no step to run next, with a notice naming the cause, and its recipes and action buttons stay enabled, a click running against the mission's path as the last successful read gave it. Work on the open mission goes on with current panes through a fault in the listing of every mission, and the run, which resolves its mission itself, refuses a path that no longer holds on its own fixed line. Actions are offered with no step to run next and against a liveness and state the extension could not confirm, so clicks must be accepted against a failed answer and a person picks a recipe without the diagram's guidance, while the window also carries the partial-page drawing and the unconfirmed-liveness reads of the option above.

Every open mission window is closed when the live read fails, and a person opens a mission again from the side-bar view once a read succeeds and lists it. No window can show or act on a state the extension cannot confirm, and the windows need no failure drawing of their own, the failure standing only in the side-bar view. A transient fault throws away every open window, with its scroll position, selected pane, and question view position, and the person must reopen each by hand; it also treats a mission whose liveness is merely unknown as the windows of ended missions are treated, a case the sibling question on the window of an ended mission settles separately.

A person then has to open each one to know which is which, which is exactly the case the question asks about. A mission tab also looks like any other untitled editor tab.

The panel's `iconPath` is one fixed icon, the same on every mission tab: either a built-in codicon through a `ThemeIcon`, which the installed API accepts and which needs no image file, or the generated activity-bar mark. open-question.question: The activity-bar icon is generated by a script from the README banner's drawing as three of its arms, a large one in the centre and a smaller one on each side. `assets/banner.txt` holds eight arms, all drawn at one character scale, a shorter and a longer kind whose heights differ by two of ten rows, and no drawing of three arms or of an arm at a larger scale exists. Which three of the eight arms does the script take, and how does the centre arm come to be larger than the two beside it?

The banner's SVG draws each character of the drawing as text in a system monospace font, in three colours, on a grid of 10 by 20 pixels per cell. The editor shows an activity-bar icon at 24 by 24 pixels in one fill colour. In what form does the icon script draw the three arms in the icon's SVG, and how much of each arm's detail (its brackets, suckers, and curl) does the icon keep at that size?
open-question.alternative: The icon script draws the three arms the way `scripts/render_banner.py` draws the banner: one `text` element per row of the arms' characters, in the same system monospace font stack on the 10 by 20 grid, scaled into the 24 by 24 icon by the SVG's `viewBox`, with every character in one fill colour instead of the three-colour mask. Every bracket, sucker, dash, and curl character of each arm is kept, and no glyph is converted to paths. It carries the banner's own recorded rendering decision (characters drawn as text in a system monospace font, no glyph converted to paths) over to the icon unchanged and can reuse the renderer's row-to-`tspan` logic almost as it stands, so the icon is the banner's drawing in the most literal sense. At 24 by 24 pixels three arms about ten columns wide and ten rows tall give each character well under one pixel of width and under two of height, so the glyphs anti-alias into an indistinct smear whose brackets and suckers cannot be told apart; and since the shape is whatever monospace font the viewer's system supplies to an SVG loaded as an image, the icon's silhouette differs from one machine to the next. How the centre arm is made larger (a scale transform or a different font size) is the three-arm derivation question's to settle.

The icon script draws every character of the three arms as filled path outlines traced from the glyphs of one fixed monospace font, placed on the drawing's cell grid and scaled into the 24 by 24 icon, in one fill colour, keeping every bracket, sucker, dash, and curl character. The icon keeps the banner's typographic look character for character while its shape no longer depends on which font the viewer's system has, so it renders identically everywhere. It needs a font file (tracked in the repository or pulled in as a dependency, with its licence) and a parser for its glyph outlines, which Python's standard library does not provide, so its viability depends on the language the icon script pipeline question settles; and at 24 pixels the outlines smear exactly as the text glyphs do, so the cost buys consistency of a mark that is still illegible in detail.

The icon script maps each character of the drawing to a small vector primitive of its own, drawn in its cell in one fill colour: `o` a dot or ring, `(` and `)` arcs, `/` and `\` diagonal strokes, `-`, `~`, `'`, `,`, `.` and `|` short strokes or ticks, so every bracket, sucker, and curl element of each arm is kept as its own shape, with no font involved. It is font-independent and deterministic like any vector form while still deriving the icon mechanically, character by character, from `assets/banner.txt`, so the icon follows the drawing if the drawing changes and needs no font file. The script must carry a hand-made shape for every character the arms use, a small glyph table that is itself new design; and at under a pixel per cell the many tiny strokes still blur together, so the per-character fidelity is mostly invisible at the size the editor shows.

The icon script reads the drawing as a grid and fills one rectangle for every non-space cell of the three arms, merged into a solid shape per arm, in one fill colour; the brackets, suckers, and curl characters all become filled cells of the same mass, so each arm keeps its overall outline (stem and curl) and none of its internal detail. It is the simplest form to generate and test, a direct and deterministic function of `banner.txt` with no font and no geometry beyond the grid, and a solid silhouette is what a one-colour 24-pixel icon reads best as. The arms come out blocky and stepped rather than as smooth tentacles, the suckers that make them read as octopus arms disappear entirely, and the 10 by 20 cell aspect stretches each step vertically, so the mark may read as three jagged bars rather than arms.

The icon script fills one rectangle for every non-space cell of the three arms in one fill colour except the sucker cells (the `o` characters, slate in the banner's colour mask), which it leaves empty as gaps in the arm; brackets and curl cells are filled, so each arm keeps its outline and its suckers as negative space. It keeps the sucker motif, the one detail that tells an octopus arm from any curved bar, while staying as simple and font-independent as the solid cell silhouette, and it turns the banner's third colour into the only form a one-colour icon can show. A sucker cell is about one pixel wide at this size, so the holes may anti-alias into a faint grey smudge or vanish on the smaller side arms, and the stepped cell edges remain; whether the holes survive depends on how large the three-arm derivation question makes each arm.

The icon script derives each arm's geometry from the drawing (the stem's centre column on each row and the path of the curl at the bottom) and draws it as one smooth stroked path, fixed or tapering in width, in one fill colour; the curl is kept as a curve, while the brackets and suckers are dropped. A single smooth curved stroke per arm stays crisp and legible at 24 pixels, matches the line weight of the editor's other activity-bar icons, and reads at a glance as three curling tentacles. The script must interpret the ASCII art as geometry (find each row's stem position and turn the curl's characters into a curve), more code with heuristics tuned to this drawing, and the result keeps the drawing's pose but none of its characters, so a change to `banner.txt` may need the heuristics revisited.

The icon script derives each arm's outline from the drawing, its edges taken from the bracket positions on each row and the curl's outer and inner edge, and draws it as a filled tapering shape in one fill colour, with each sucker cut out as a small round hole (an even-odd or masked sub-path); the brackets survive as the shape's edge, the curl as its curled end, and the suckers as holes, for all three arms alike. It is the most recognisable form of an octopus arm a one-colour icon can carry, a smooth filled tentacle with visible suckers, and it uses all three kinds of the drawing's detail rather than discarding any. It needs the most geometry of any option, edges and curl traced from characters plus hole placement, and on the two smaller side arms the holes come out around a pixel or less, so they may blur into the fill and add generation cost for detail only the centre arm can show; how much smaller the side arms are is the three-arm derivation question's to settle.

The icon script derives each arm's outline from the drawing as a filled tapering shape with its curl, in one fill colour, and grades the detail by arm size: the large centre arm keeps its suckers as round holes cut out of the fill, while the two smaller side arms are drawn as plain silhouettes with no holes; brackets survive only as the shapes' edges. open-question.question: The banner's SVG is a tracked file regenerated by hand with `scripts/render_banner.py`, a stdlib-only Python script, and pinned to that script's output by `tests/test_banner.py`. alternative.id: Python sibling script, tracked, pytest pin

open-question.alternative: A new stdlib-only Python script beside the banner renderer at the repository root, `scripts/render_icon.py`, run by hand like `scripts/render_banner.py` and leaving that script unchanged. It reads `assets/banner.txt` and writes the icon as a tracked SVG inside the extension's own directory (for example `gurita-vscode/media/`), where the manifest's `viewsContainers` entry can name it and the VSIX carries it, since `assets/` lies outside the packaged root. A new pytest test under `tests/`, shaped like `tests/test_banner.py`, loads the script and asserts that the tracked icon is well-formed SVG and equals what the script renders from the drawing, so CI's two pytest runs catch a stale icon. It repeats a pipeline the project already runs and tests: the banner's recorded decision (a plain-text drawing as the source of truth and an SVG generated by a script run by hand) carries over unchanged, the icon is in every checkout with no build step, and the pin runs in CI, which runs pytest but no Node tests. The icon becomes a second derived file someone must remember to regenerate after any change to the drawing, caught only by a failing test, and a script outside `gurita-vscode/` produces a file inside it, so the extension's directory no longer holds everything that builds it, and the change needs CLAUDE.md's repository layout and the render-banner command line updated.

alternative.id: Folded into render_banner.py, tracked, pinned in test_banner

open-question.alternative: The icon is produced by `scripts/render_banner.py` itself, the stdlib-only Python renderer, so one run by hand writes both `assets/banner.svg` and the tracked icon inside `gurita-vscode/` (for example `gurita-vscode/media/`), reusing its drawing and colour-mask parsing. `tests/test_banner.py` is extended to assert that the tracked icon is well-formed SVG and equals the script's output, so the existing CI pytest runs pin both files. A drawing edit followed by the one documented command regenerates the banner and the icon together, so the two can never drift apart in a checkout, and the parsing of `banner.txt` stays in one place under one test file. It changes the contract of a finished mission's tool, which today takes any drawing path and writes only `<stem>.svg` beside it, by giving it a fixed second output in another directory. Its fit also depends on the axis the icon-mark-form question owns: an icon drawn in a form other than the banner's monospace text would put two unrelated renderers in one file.

A stdlib-only Python script under the repository's `scripts/`, run by hand, writes the icon as a tracked SVG inside `gurita-vscode/` for the manifest to name, and no test compares the tracked icon with the script's output. It is the least machinery: one script and one committed file, with no new test, no package-time step, and nothing for CI to keep green, which suits an icon that changes only when the drawing does. Nothing catches a drawing edit or a hand edit of the icon that was not regenerated, so the icon can silently stop being the script's output, unlike the banner, which the project chose to pin.

alternative.id: Node in bundle.js, package-time, no pin

open-question.alternative: The icon is generated in Node by the extension's own build step, `gurita-vscode/scripts/bundle.js` (or a sibling script it calls), which already reads files from the repository root at every package. open-question.alternative: The same package-time pipeline as rendering in `bundle.js`: Node code under `gurita-vscode/scripts/` writes the icon from `assets/banner.txt` into the git-ignored `gurita-vscode/bundled/` at every package, and the manifest names it there.
